subject: Environment
topic: Wetlands and Ramsar sites — mixed tiers
description: Ramsar Convention, Indian wetlands, Montreux Record, wetland ecology

questions.stem: The Ramsar Convention on Wetlands was signed in 1971 at:

options.option_text: Rio de Janeiro, Brazil
Ramsar, Iran
Stockholm, Sweden
Nairobi, Kenya

questions.explanation: The Convention was signed on 2 February 1971 in the Iranian city of Ramsar on the Caspian Sea — hence the name. It came into force in 1975. 2 February is observed as World Wetlands Day. India joined in 1982 and — as of early 2026 — has over 85 Ramsar sites, the largest network in Asia.

questions.stem: Chilika Lake — the largest brackish-water lagoon in India — lies in which state?

options.option_text: Andhra Pradesh
Odisha
Tamil Nadu
West Bengal

questions.explanation: Chilika — on the east coast in Odisha — was India's first Ramsar site (1981). Area ~1,100 km² (varies seasonally). Home to the Irrawaddy dolphin, vast flocks of migratory birds, and the endangered Barkudia limbless skink. Removed from the Montreux Record in 2002 after successful rejuvenation — a rare success story cited at international forums.

questions.stem: The 'Montreux Record' maintained under the Ramsar Convention is a list of:

options.option_text: Wetlands of international importance under threat
Wetlands that have lost their protected status
Wetlands used for commercial fishing
Wetlands created by human activity

questions.explanation: The Montreux Record (established 1990) is a register of Ramsar-listed wetlands where ecological character has changed, is changing, or is likely to change due to pollution, human interference, or other factors. India currently has two sites on the Record — Keoladeo National Park (Bharatpur, Rajasthan) and Loktak Lake (Manipur). Chilika was the only site ever removed (2002) after restoration.

questions.stem: Loktak Lake — famous for its floating 'phumdis' (vegetation masses) — is situated in:

options.option_text: Meghalaya
Manipur
Mizoram
Nagaland

questions.explanation: Loktak — the largest freshwater lake in North-East India — is in Manipur. Its phumdis host Keibul Lamjao National Park, the only floating national park in the world, and the last habitat of the Sangai (Rucervus eldii eldii), Manipur's state animal (also called the dancing deer or brow-antlered deer). Loktak is on the Montreux Record due to siltation and the Ithai barrage's ecological impact.

questions.stem: Keoladeo National Park — a Ramsar site and UNESCO World Heritage site — is located in:

options.option_text: Gujarat
Rajasthan
Madhya Pradesh
Haryana

questions.explanation: Keoladeo (formerly Bharatpur Bird Sanctuary) — Bharatpur, Rajasthan — is a man-made wetland created by the Maharaja of Bharatpur in the 19th century. Winter home to thousands of waterfowl; was the only known wintering site of the Siberian crane in India (last confirmed sighting 2002). Declared a National Park in 1982, UNESCO World Heritage site 1985, Ramsar site 1981. Currently on the Montreux Record over water-shortage issues.

questions.stem: Wetlands are often called the 'kidneys of the landscape' because they:

options.option_text: Store large amounts of groundwater
Filter pollutants and purify water
Produce oxygen from photosynthesis
Regulate atmospheric temperature

questions.explanation: Wetlands trap sediments, absorb excess nutrients (nitrogen, phosphorus), and break down pollutants through microbial action — similar to kidneys filtering blood. Other ecosystem services: flood control (storm-water buffer), groundwater recharge, carbon sequestration (mangroves, peatlands store huge carbon), biodiversity refuge, fisheries support, shoreline stabilisation. 'Kidneys of the landscape' is a phrase coined by American ecologist William J. Mitsch.

questions.stem: Under the Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2017, the authority responsible for notifying and managing wetlands at the state level is the:

options.option_text: Central Pollution Control Board
State Wetland Authority
Ministry of Jal Shakti
National Biodiversity Authority

questions.explanation: The 2017 Rules — replacing the 2010 rules — decentralised management. Each State / UT sets up a State Wetland Authority (SWA), chaired by the environment minister, to identify and notify wetlands, regulate activities, and maintain a Brief Document per wetland. Prohibited activities: conversion for non-wetland uses, setting up / expanding industries, solid-waste dumping, untreated effluent discharge. The National Wetland Committee (under MoEFCC) provides oversight.

questions.stem: As of 2023, which Indian state has the HIGHEST number of Ramsar-designated wetland sites within its territory?

options.option_text: Uttar Pradesh, with sites like Nawabganj and Sur Sarovar
Tamil Nadu, with 14 designated Ramsar wetland sites
Odisha, known for Chilika Lake and Bhitarkanika mangroves
Rajasthan, home to Sambhar Salt Lake and Keoladeo Ghana

questions.explanation: Tamil Nadu leads all Indian states with 14 Ramsar-designated sites, including Point Calimere, Vedanthangal, Pallikaranai Marsh, and Kazhuveli. Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh have multiple Ramsar sites but fewer than Tamil Nadu. Odisha's well-known Chilika accounts for only one site.

questions.stem: 'World Wetlands Day' is observed globally on 2nd February every year. This date marks the anniversary of which event?

options.option_text: Signing of the Ramsar Convention on Wetlands at Ramsar, Iran in 1971
Formation of the International Union for Conservation of Nature at Fontainebleau
Adoption of the Convention on Biological Diversity in Nairobi, Kenya
Establishment of the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) in Nairobi

questions.explanation: The Ramsar Convention on Wetlands was adopted on 2 February 1971 at Ramsar, Iran; World Wetlands Day has been marked on this date since 1997. The CBD (Option C) was adopted at Rio Earth Summit in 1992. UNEP was established in June 1972. Both are common distractors due to environmental association.

questions.stem: Tsomoriri Lake — a Ramsar-designated high-altitude wetland and a critical breeding habitat for the Bar-headed Goose — is situated in which region of India?

options.option_text: Sikkim, near the Kanchenjunga Biosphere Reserve boundary
Ladakh, at an elevation of approximately 4,522 metres above sea level
Himachal Pradesh, close to the Spiti Valley cold desert zone
Uttarakhand, adjacent to the Valley of Flowers National Park

questions.explanation: Tsomoriri (Moriri Lake) lies in the Changthang plateau of Ladakh at ~4,522 m, making it one of the highest Ramsar sites globally. It was designated in 2002. Spiti (HP) and Sikkim are common confusions because both have high-altitude lakes (Chandratal, Gurudongmar), but Tsomoriri is exclusively in Ladakh.

questions.stem: Harike Wetland (Hari-ke-Pattan), a Ramsar site formed at the confluence of the Beas and Sutlej rivers, falls administratively in which Indian state?

options.option_text: Haryana, in the districts of Kurukshetra and Karnal
Himachal Pradesh, within the upper Kangra valley watershed
Punjab, spread across Ferozepur and Tarn Taran districts
Rajasthan, bordering the Bikaner semi-arid dune ecosystem

questions.explanation: Harike Wetland, designated a Ramsar site in 1990, lies in Punjab at the Beas–Sutlej confluence straddling Ferozepur and Tarn Taran districts. It is India's largest wetland in the northwest plains. Haryana is a plausible distractor because it borders Punjab; Himachal Pradesh is tempting since the Beas originates there, but the wetland itself is in Punjab.

questions.stem: Under Ramsar Criterion 5, a wetland qualifies as internationally important if it regularly supports at least how many individual waterbirds?

options.option_text: At least 10,000 individual waterbirds counted in any season
At least 50,000 individual waterbirds counted in any season
At least 5,000 individual waterbirds counted in any season
At least 20,000 individual waterbirds counted in any season

questions.explanation: Ramsar Criterion 5 specifies 20,000 or more waterbirds as the threshold for international importance. 10,000 (Option A) is the most frequent wrong recall. Criterion 6 is a separate standard requiring support of 1% of a species' global population — distinct from the absolute-number criterion tested here.

questions.stem: The Ramsar Convention's 'Wise Use' principle is formally defined within the convention framework as which of the following?

options.option_text: Complete protection ensuring zero human activity within designated Ramsar site boundaries
Sustainable use that prevents any change to the wetland's natural hydrological cycle
Maintenance of ecological character via ecosystem approaches within sustainable development
Restoration of degraded wetlands to their original pre-disturbance ecological condition

questions.explanation: Ramsar formally defines Wise Use as 'the maintenance of their ecological character, achieved through the implementation of ecosystem approaches, within the context of sustainable development.' It explicitly permits sustainable human use — Option A (zero human activity) contradicts this. Option D describes ecological restoration, which is related but a separate concept not constituting the Wise Use definition.

questions.stem: Deepor Beel — a Ramsar site in Assam placed on the Montreux Record — faces a critical structural threat from an infrastructure corridor bisecting its core wetland zone. This corridor is a:

options.option_text: Railway line of the Northeast Frontier Railway cutting across the wetland
National highway flyover constructed to reduce vehicle–wildlife conflict
High-tension power transmission line supplying the Meghalaya border districts
Petroleum pipeline connecting the Digboi refinery to Guwahati terminal

questions.explanation: Deepor Beel's primary infrastructure threat is the Northeast Frontier Railway track that physically cuts through the wetland, combined with municipal solid waste dumping from Guwahati — reasons it was included in the Montreux Record (Ramsar sites facing adverse ecological change). A highway (Option B) exists nearby but is not the documented bisecting corridor recorded in the Ramsar threat assessment.
